Title: Toward a Theory of the Evolution of the Global Political Economy: Exploring the Effect of ‘Varieties of Capitalism’ on Equality and Sustainability
Abstract: This paper explores wealth and environmental inequalities which arise from global wealth creation and distribution dynamics.  The primary independent variable which explains these dynamics among advanced political economies is the institutionally-based ‘variety of capitalism’: liberal market economies (LMEs) vs coordinated market economies (CMEs).  LMEs like the US and UK are demonstrated to be built for growth and efficiency which thrive in high economic growth rate environments, while CMEs like Japan, Germany (and to a large degree, France) are demonstrated to be built for equality and sustainability which thrive in low economic growth rate environments.  Over the past 50 years, LMEs are shown to have increased their efficiency or wealth creation, at the expense of equality, whereas CMEs are shown to have increased their efficiency while simultaneously increasing equality.  In addition, CMEs are empirically demonstrated to have higher levels of sustainability (e.g. as measured by CO2), where LMEs focus on ‘green growth’ and adaptation, while CMEs focus on ‘de-growth’ and mitigation.  In fact, the institutional configuration which generates higher equality is also that which appears to generate higher sustainability.  A mathematical model of the evolution of the global political is presented which captures global competition between LMEs and CMEs as a multi-species, predator-prey system with LMEs and CMEs being the multi-species of competing ‘predators’ consuming the global carrying capacity of sustaining resources or ‘prey’.  The dynamic stock-flow-feedback structural model is constructed using a system of simultaneous first-order, nonlinear, autonomous, homogeneous ordinary differential equations.  Econometric analysis of longitudinal and panel datasets is used to estimate model input parameters as well as to calibrate and validate model output state variables. Because of the nonlinearities and high-dimensional state spaces, the equations of motion are converted to finite difference equations and the transitional dynamics are simulated numerically using explicit fourth-order Runge-Kutta integration.  The model mathematically derives and numerically simulates the Piketty inequality equation and supports other findings of the World Inequality Lab’s research on wealth and environmental inequalities.

Title: Redistribution, Taxes, and Gender Gaps: Evidence from Top Income Adjustments in Chile
Abstract: Access to tax data has transformed the study of inequality by enabling corrections to household surveys and improving the identification of top incomes. Despite this progress, relatively little attention has been paid to the broader consequences of survey adjustments beyond aggregate inequality measures. This study addresses that gap by examining two adjustment methodologies applied to Chile’s CASEN household survey and assessing their implications for income taxation and gender disparities. Using administrative records from the Chilean Internal Revenue Service, we show that while aggregate inequality measures differ only marginally across methods, gender disaggregated adjustments reveal important nuances. In particular, separate adjustments for men and women allow for the identification of a small group of high income women whose presence is obscured in aggregate corrections. This leads to a measurable increase in female representation within the top decile of incomes. These findings underscore the importance of tailoring survey adjustments to specific research objectives, particularly subgroup analysis, and contribute to a deeper understanding of inequality and tax distribution from a gender perspective.

Title: Equality and Development: A Comparative & Historical Perspective 1800-2025
Abstract: This paper uses extended series on income and wealth inequality from the World Inequality Database (WID) covering all world regions over the 1800-2025 period, together with new series on hourly productivity and human capital expenditure, to revisit the relationship between equality and development, with a much broader comparative and historical perspective than previous studies. Over the long-run, we find a strong positive association between equality and productivity. Our proposed interpretation is that the rise of inclusive “social-democratic” institutions (including extended access to human capital, public services and democratic participation) led both to more equality and higher productivity, particularly in Western and Nordic Europe. We discuss the implications for future sustainable development strategies.
